title: Artist Vija Celmins and director Denis Villeneuve honored at star-studded LACMA Art+Film Gala.
summary: The Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA) hosted its 15th annual Art+Film Gala on November 7, honoring artist Vija Celmins and filmmaker Denis Villeneuve. The event, co-chaired by LACMA trustee Eva Chow and Leonardo DiCaprio, welcomed more than 600 guests and raised nearly $7 million, a record for the event. These funds will go towards the museum’s film initiatives and broader programming. The evening featured a performance by musical guest ROSÉ, including the live debut of her new single “New Trick.” “It was a privilege to recognize the extraordinary careers of Vija Celmins and Denis Villeneuve, whose work can alter our perception of the visual world or transport us to worlds of the imagination,” said Michael Govan , director of the museum. Celmins, accepting her honor, reflected on how Los Angeles shaped her meticulous renderings of oceans, deserts, and night skies. “Los Angeles had a big influence on me. I had never lived next to the ocean, and I had never seen the land, and it sort of crept into my work,” she recalled. Villeneuve, introduced by Nicole Kidman, said, “When a museum, a temple for artists, welcomes a filmmaker and puts the spotlight on cinema, it means a great deal to me. Especially this museum, because LACMA has already given me so much.” Chow, who has co-chaired the gala for all 15 of its editions, used the evening to announce that this would be her final year in the role. “Seeing the gala become one of Los Angeles’s most celebrated traditions has been one of the great privileges of my life,” she said. “I leave this chapter with tremendous pride, and above all, gratitude. I hope the gala will continue to grow and inspire future generations, bringing together the world of art and film for many years to come.” Govan paid tribute to Chow ahead of the announcement, crediting her with bringing together “so many artists, filmmakers, designers, and creatives.” Guests arrived against the backdrop of Chris Burden ’s Urban Light (2008)—the museum’s iconic outdoor installation of a forest of streetlights—for a cocktail reception before dinner overlooking Michael Heizer ’s Levitated Mass (2012). Govan also used the evening to announce the installation of Shio Kusaka ’s Beam , a new public sculpture on the museum’s terrace, made possible by the trustees’ support. Artists in attendance included Ed Ruscha , Catherine Opie , Jacqueline Humphries , Kenny Scharf , Mickalene Thomas , Lauren Halsey , Refik Anadol , and Christina Quarles . Other celebrities at the event included Timothée Chalamet, Kim Kardashian, Viola Davis, Andrew Garfield, Salma Hayek Pinault, Olivia Munn, Al Pacino, Sarah Paulson, Anya Taylor-Joy, Emma Watson, and Paris Hilton, among hundreds of others from film, fashion, and music. The red carpet brought its own share of standout fashion, with Gucci —the night’s presenting sponsor—turning out custom looks for model Alex Consani, in a sculptural black gown; model and musician Soo Joo Park, in a feathered dress; and writer and curator Antwaun Sargent, in an intricately detailed ensemble. Kylie Jenner wore a brown-and-silver deer-print gown from Ashi Studio’s spring/summer 2026 couture collection, while ROSÉ performed in custom Saint Laurent .

title: Indian artist Arpita Singh dies at 89
summary: Arpita Singh , the modernist painter whose dense, densely populated canvases traced the inner and political lives of Indian women across six decades, died Monday at Fortis Hospital in New Delhi. She was 89. Her husband, the artist Paramjit Singh , told the Press Trust of India the cause was an age-related ailment. “She had heart and lung-related issues for some years now,” Paramjit said. “However, she was actively working. Her health dipped in the last three days, and she was admitted to the hospital.” Singh was born in 1937 in Baranagar, in what is now West Bengal in India. She grew up amid India’s struggle for independence and the violent 1947 partition, themes that would recur throughout her work. Later, major national inflection points, including the 1975 state of emergency and the economic liberalization of the 1990s, also shaped her worldview. She went to art school on the advice of her high school principal, earning a diploma in fine arts from Delhi Polytechnic in 1959. She went on to work as a textile designer at the Weavers' Service Centre, a postwar government institution that shaped the early careers of numerous Indian modernists. There, she absorbed the narrative folk traditions, including pattachitra scroll painting and kantha embroidery, which would become lifelong influences alongside Bengali poetry and Western Surrealism . She began painting and, in the 1960s, emerged as part of India's modernist art movement . Singh’s paintings were commonly built around an ambiguous female protagonist, surrounded by fragmented texts, flowers, vehicles, and domestic objects of everyday urban Indian life. Often rendered in thick, layered oil paint across crowded, gravity-less pictorial planes, these paintings were compared by critics to South Asian miniature painting and to maps. “I always paint the things I see and experience every day,” she told curator Hans Ulrich Obrist in an interview for the catalogue of her 2025 Serpentine Galleries survey. “They’re almost the same every day.” In works like My Lollipop City: Gemini Rising (2005), bureaucratic figures stand atop a map of New Delhi annotated with road names and constellations, a corner of the canvas warning, in the artist’s own hand, “THE MAP IS FAULTY DO NOT FOLLOW IT.” Her 1993 painting My Mother , among her best-known, divides the canvas along a diagonal road, with a half-length portrait of her mother facing a crowded field of cars, bicycles, soldiers, and crosses. Singh received the Padma Bhushan, India’s third-highest civilian honor, in 2011, and the Lalit Kala Akademi Fellowship in 2014. Her work is held in the collections of the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi, the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, and the Peabody Essex Museum.She is represented in New Delhi by Vadehra Art Gallery . In 2024, her work appeared alongside that of longtime peers Nilima Sheikh , Nalini Malani , and Madhvi Parekh in “The Imaginary Institution of India: Art 1975–1998” at London’s Barbican Centre. The following year, the Serpentine North presented “Remembering,” a 60-year survey and Singh’s first institutional solo exhibition outside India , co-organized with Obrist, the Serpentine’s artistic director, who called her an inspiration to “five generations of Indian contemporary artists.” Roshini Vadehra, her longtime gallerist, said the growing international attention reflected a broader moment for Indian art, driven by “a blend of historical traditions and contemporary relevance that speaks to global concerns: identity, politics, gender, and social transformation.” Her market saw momentum, too. A 16-panel mural-scale work, The Wish Dream (2001), sold for $2.24 million at a Saffronart auction in 2010, a record at the time for a living Indian woman artist. News of Singh’s death drew tributes across the Indian art world. The curator Uma Nair called her “the high priestess of contemporary Indian art” and “the female M.F. Husain of the female arc,” praising the way she “wove violence and chaos and patriarchal mores all so softly.” The poet Ashok Vajpeyi, managing trustee of the Raza Foundation, wrote that “her art survives her life and would now create a new posthumous life of itself.” Singh is survived by her husband. Their only daughter, the artist Anjum Singh, died of cancer in 2020.

title: This Radical Art Collection Is a Sign of Texas’s Reinvention
summary: In some ways, it was the type of event that happens everywhere in the international art world: a convivial gathering of well-heeled guests, free-flowing drinks, and representatives from major galleries including Lisson , Edel Assanti, and Thaddaeus Ropac . In others, it was unmistakably Texan: hefty picanha steaks sizzled over an open fire, while a honky-tonk band provided the soundtrack. Such was the opening of Ostillo, a new art foundation in Austin that opened in September, where, the following evening, at a lavish dinner, artist and musician Lonnie Holley performed live. Between the caliber of the attendees, the scale of the hospitality, and the art itself, the occasion marked an ambitious new arrival on the Austin art scene. It’s a telling moment for a city that has been transforming for years, and for a state entering a new political chapter after November’s midterms delivered Texas Democrats their first statewide victories since 1994. Austin, long celebrated for its independent music scene and laid-back character, has become a magnet for technology companies, wealth, and new residents. Soho House opened on South Congress Avenue in 2021, while the city’s cultural institutions have grown in size and status. The Blanton Museum of Art unveiled its redesigned grounds in 2023, and the Emma S. Barrientos Mexican American Cultural Center reopened following a major expansion this June. Against this backdrop, Ostillo represents another dimension of Austin’s transformation: a foundation dedicated to showing challenging contemporary art, free of charge. It grew out of the collection of local real estate developer René Campos, who, with the help of Paris-based art advisor and founding director Sacha Zerbib, has spent the last decade assembling more than 90 works. Zerbib and Campos first met in Paris in 2016 through a shared interest in architecture. Although Campos had long been fascinated by history and art, he had yet to begin collecting seriously. “Every time he steps into a new place, the first thing he goes to is a museum,” Zerbib said. “That is the kind of mindset he has: always ready to learn.” Their first acquisition together was something of a test of Campos’s appetite for experimentation: a monumental, 2.5-meter-wide stripe painting by German artist Günther Förg . Hardly an obvious starting point, it established a relationship built on trust and a willingness to venture into unfamiliar territory. “Very early on I understood that he was not going to go for the eye-candy kind of works, the easily accessible, entertaining art,” Zerbib said. “It was more about a certain darkness, a certain seriousness that the art was going to convey.” That sensibility is evident in Ostillo’s inaugural exhibition, “Masquerade,” on view through spring 2027, which brings together works by artists including Glenn Ligon , Sylvia Snowden , Sanya Kantarovsky , Mohammed Sami , Salman Toor , and Christopher Wool . The exhibition takes its name from Ligon’s Masquerade (2006), a work incorporating text from James Baldwin’s essay “Stranger in the Village.” Exploring identity, displacement, and the ways people conceal or reveal themselves, the show reflects a collection concerned with confronting uncomfortable questions about the human experience. For Zerbib, the guiding principle is “radicality,” which he defines as “uncompromising works” that don’t shy away from difficult ideas, many of which are referenced in the foundation’s very location. Ostillo occupies a transformed industrial building in Rosewood, a historically Black neighborhood of East Austin. The city’s 1928 master plan helped institutionalize racial segregation by concentrating services for Black residents in East Austin. More recently, rapid development and rising property values have reshaped the neighborhood, with modern buildings an increasingly common sight amid the historical surroundings. A brand-new contemporary art foundation here adds another layer to this story of change. Zerbib himself draws a connection between the exhibition’s themes of migration and displacement and Texas’s own complicated history, including slavery and forced migration. The parallels were not intentional, he says, but have become increasingly apparent as the collection has taken shape. Ostillo is also seeking to connect with the neighborhood beyond its exhibition walls. Free to visit, it includes a public library and an outdoor performance space that will serve as the permanent home of the East Side Kings Festival, celebrating the area’s musical heritage. Zerbib has been working with other Austin institutions such as the Blanton Museum of Art and The Contemporary Austin to help Ostillo find its place in the city’s cultural landscape. “As soon as they understood the artists that I was intending to show, they immediately took it seriously,” he recalled. According to Zerbib, Campos decided he wanted to present his collection publicly as early as 2018. “We realized that what we had already acquired was too impactful not to be shared with the public,” he said. There is something characteristically Texan about the impulse. Zerbib sees the foundation as an extension of Campos’s generosity: the same instinct that sees him welcome guests to his ranch and enthusiastically show them around the property for opening weekend. “Texas has something about generosity, hospitality, community, and they love sharing everything,” Zerbib said. Some things, it seems, don’t change, no matter what the political climate.

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Leon Xu
summary: For Leon Xu , a painting begins with a physical sensation, what he calls “brain tingles.” Whenever he feels that, Xu takes a photo to capture the moment. From these snapshots, the New York–based artist transforms ordinary slices of city life—neon signs, bodega flowers, old cars, the view from a window—into hazy, luminous paintings that strike a balance between real memories and imagined ones. “My work is about the distance between experiencing something and trying to remember it after time has gone by,” he explained. “By the time I’m painting it, it’s already three layers removed from the original moment. It’s almost like a more vivid new thing.” This is not a goodbye, 2026 Leon Xu Mai 36 Galerie Send me an Angel, 2026 Leon Xu Mai 36 Galerie Xu grew up painting, with a photographer father who helped shape his eye. In the studio, he keeps his reference photos in his peripheral vision, glancing at them only occasionally, if needed. His technique, airbrush layered with brushwork, reflects his teenage years making graffiti in San Francisco, Born in Zhongshan, China, and raised in San Francisco, Xu moved to New York in 2019. Today, he works from a Chinatown studio, chosen for its proximity to the streets that inspire him. His daily walks in the neighborhood yield subjects ranging from takeout spots to jewelry displays. Muah!, 2026 Leon Xu Mai 36 Galerie Xu’s career took off during the pandemic, when he began painting daily and sharing his work on Instagram. In 2022, he had his first solo exhibition with Zürich’s Mai 36 Galerie , “Wishful Thinking,” followed by “ Afterglow ” in 2025. The gallery announced its representation of Xu in July 2026 and will have presented his work at Art Basel, ARCOmadrid, ACK Kyoto, and Art Basel Miami Beach 2026 this year. A major painting will enter the collection of the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, in December. We caught up with Xu at his Chinatown studio and joined him on his daily walk, before learning about what drives his paintings. Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Diambe
summary: For Brazilian artist Diambe , the natural world is both material and subject. They cast bronze from beeswax, paint in egg tempera on linen, and color their sculptures and paintings with mineral pigments derived from stones. “The way that things change in nature and how we’re all subjected to forces that we cannot control properly is something that I try to make evident in my work,” Diambe told us. Mañana estaré lejos, 2025 Diambe Simões de Assis Qualidade do ar, 2025 Diambe Simões de Assis They cast bronze from beeswax, paint in egg tempera on linen, and color their sculptures and paintings with pigments derived from minerals. “The way that things change in nature and how we’re all subjected to forces that we cannot control properly is something that I try to make evident in my work,” Diambe told us. Born in Rio de Janeiro and based in São Paulo, Diambe transforms delicate, impermanent beeswax sculptures into enduring bronze. They’ve tied the wax’s melting point to extreme heat-index readings in Brazil, bringing climate change into their process. Diambe’s career has gained considerable momentum in the past few years. “Bees beings beans,” their largest solo exhibition to date, opened at Kunsthalle Basel in early 2026. It followed a solo booth at Frieze London in 2025 with Simões de Assis . And this week, Diambe unveils two new exhibitions: a two-artist show with Tunji Adeniyi-Jones opening November 10th at Simões de Assis in Curitiba, Brazil, and a solo show opening November 11th at kaufmann repetto in Milan. title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Danielle Fretwell
summary: At first glance, Danielle Fretwell ’s paintings look like lavish feasts. Fish, berries, flowers, silverware, and antique linens are rendered in rich detail, recalling the still lifes of the Dutch Golden Age . Some are alluring arrangements of objects and delicacies, while others depict banquet scenes partially obscured by swaths of abstraction, creating a push and pull between what’s revealed and what’s hidden. “I have an interest in truth and what it takes for someone to trust something or someone,” the New Hampshire–based artist told us. Second Nature, 2026 Danielle Fretwell Alice Amati Set Piece, 2026 Danielle Fretwell Alice Amati In her “split still lifes,” Fretwell meticulously stages and photographs her arrangements before rendering them in oil paint on large canvases. She then adds a layer of thinned paint, pressing sheets and foam into the wet surface to create an abstract veil of color. “I try to create spaces that are a bit difficult for the viewer to enter, hoping that sparks a sense of discomfort,” she explained. Her compositions suggest a sumptuous meal about to begin, one the viewer will never fully witness. Fretwell finds the tableware, candlesticks, and linens in her paintings at antique shops. “I think that I’m really drawn to objects that have a tension between attraction and repulsion,” she told us. “I love the cycle and circulation of objects and how objects long outlive the people who once owned them.” Dissonance, 2026 Danielle Fretwell Alice Amati Fretwell earned her MFA from Boston University in 2021, and the years since have brought a steady run of firsts. She is represented by Alice Amati in London, where she had her first solo exhibition, “ Shallow Invitations ,” in 2024, followed by a solo booth at NADA New York in 2025 and a second solo show with the gallery, “ Tablescapes ,” that fall. This summer, she made her New York solo debut with “ Terms of Consumption ” at Olney Gleason , and Alice Amati recently presented her work at Artissima in Turin. We caught up with Fretwell in New Hampshire, joining her on a hunt for antique candlesticks before heading back to her home studio, where she showed us how she builds her compositions and paints them. title: How to Collect Small Sculpture, According to Experts
summary: Small-scale sculpture has a serious history. In the ancient world, handheld sculptures often served as votive objects or fertility icons, central to both ritual and personal life. During the Renaissance, maquettes—small-scale studies for larger sculptures—became a key step in the development of the era’s artworks. In the 20th century, meanwhile, the likes of Alberto Giacometti ’s evocative figures and Constantin Brâncuși ’s studies and small-scale works helped revolutionize modern sculpture. Collecting tabletop sculpture comes with its own pleasures and peculiarities, factoring in display, scale, and context. These are objects that can live in personal spaces—on coffee tables or bookshelves—and thrive in stand-alone settings. Such nuances and choices are what lend small sculptures their power and complexity. “You don’t just look at a tabletop sculpture from one direction. You walk around it and notice how the light changes its surface, and discover details over time,” said Raimonda Ameti, director at Antwerp gallery Objects With Narratives . The hurdles in buying smaller sculptures are often more psychological than practical. Sotiris Sotiriou, founder of COMA in Sydney, calls the main barrier “confidence rather than price.” Elizabeth Feld, director at Hirschl & Adler , is more to the point. “People are terrified of knocking things over,” she said. Understanding materials For some would-be collectors, understanding material and medium can feel opaque and daunting. It need not be. While small-scale sculpture can be made from a dazzling range of materials, most works can be categorized as one of the following: bronze and cast metal , ceramics , stone , glass , wood , or assemblage —which often mixes different media. In terms of display, these works don’t require too much specialized care, but each has its own unique qualities to consider. Bronze and cast metal sculptures are, for instance, among the oldest sculptural materials, dating back to the ancient world. Artists and collectors continue to embrace them today. “With bronze, you want to understand the casting and patina,” said Ameti. Asking the seller whether the artist or a specialist foundry made the piece is a smart ask, she notes. One of the hottest collecting categories today, ceramic and clay range from hand-built one-offs to kiln-fired editions. The unique and unpredictable qualities of fired works are what often appeal; a kind of magic transformation takes place in the kiln. The experts Artsy spoke to advise collectors to examine the glaze, the surface, and how the piece was fired. “We’ve seen considerable interest in ceramics and works that foreground their material qualities,” said Sotiriou. “I think part of this comes from an increasing appreciation for process and craft. Collectors are interested in understanding how something was made, whether that’s the unpredictability of a ceramic firing, the physicality of carving stone, or the transformation involved in casting bronze.” While stone sculptures are rarer at a tabletop scale, they’re worth seeking out, as marble and alabaster have a weight and permanence other materials lack. For these materials, which can be fragile, ask the gallery about handling and care. Off To See The Wizard, 2025 Hedy Yang Galerie Robertson Arès Neighborling Maquette 25, 2025 Seth Clark Paradigm Gallery + Studio For a more affordable entry point, resin and glass can be accessible. Quality can vary widely, however, so check clarity and surface finish, and whether any edition is properly documented. Found and assembled objects are a distinct tradition in which meaning is often inseparable from the materials, so ask the seller or artist what was used and why. “We always encourage people to ask questions about how a work was made,” said Ameti. But don’t hold out for perfection. Irregularities and marks can be what make a work special, as long as they are intentional. Ameti sees growing interest in ceramics, bronze, and stone, driven by buyers who want to see the maker’s hand, with its texture, imperfections, and process. Sotiriou offers a useful test for any of them: is the material necessary to the work, and is the artist doing something compelling with it? How to live with small sculpture Untitled, 2026 Yuji Ueda COMA Unlike a framed work, which arrives with its own border, tabletop sculpture depends heavily on its setting. The galleries we spoke to advised starting with scale. A work that is too small vanishes on a large console, and one that is too large crowds it. A general rule is that a sculpture should occupy a third to half the depth of the surface, meaning a shelf that’s 12-inches deep could be home to a work with a 6-inch footprint, whereas a 36-inch coffee table might look best with a sculpture measuring about a foot wide. Of course, the ultimate aesthetic test for what looks right is the collector’s eye. “A small sculpture doesn’t necessarily require much physical space, but it does benefit from visual space,” said Sotiriou. Ameti agrees, saying not to overcrowd an environment: “A small sculpture doesn’t need much room, but it does need a bit of breathing space. You don’t want it to disappear between too many other objects.” A good rule of thumb is to choose a spot that offers several angles, such as a shelf or console you pass daily, without over-optimizing for one view. Feld recalls advising a client on a pair of entry-hall niches, where the planned built-in wooden pedestals pulled attention away from the works and left the space feeling cold and stilted. “Once we removed the bases and selected sculptures that were freestanding, the space became welcoming, warm, and interactive,” she said. Ameti tells collectors to remember they are living in a home. “We also don’t believe sculpture should always be displayed on a pedestal or treated like something in a museum,” she said. Torso, about 1988 Elizabeth Catlett Hirschl & Adler Fragment 1, 2021 Maria Elena González Hirschl & Adler Light matters just as much. “A work of art can either come alive or get totally overlooked by the right or the wrong—or a lack of—lighting,” said Feld. Light exposure from the side reveals texture in ceramic and bronze, while direct overhead light can flatten a work, so try moving a small lamp until it lights the piece from slightly to the side. Check it in daylight and in evening light too. With children or pets at home, look for a bookshelf or niche where a work is unlikely to be knocked over. Finally, consider whether to show a piece alone or in a group. A single strong work can read better alone, and groupings work when something connects them, such as material, scale, palette, or maker. Feld has seen “more is more” rooms succeed when every object is special, but avoid a shelf of unrelated things competing for attention. Assessing value No matter the material that a sculpture is made of, one should always buy the best quality work of art they can afford at a given moment,” Feld said. “Not only will this guarantee survival over time, but it will help to maintain the value of what they have invested in a work.” Like all media, prices for tabletop sculptures can vary widely. Under $500, the experts say to look for ceramic and resin by emerging makers, or open editions by established artists. From $500 to $2,500—the most active range for serious collectors—you’ll find original ceramics, small bronze editions, and cast works by gallery-represented artists. From $2,500 to $10,000, expect signed, numbered editions in bronze or ceramic by established names and unique hand-built works by represented artists. Above that, you’re looking at unique or rare editions by established artists that can veer into blue-chip names such as Giacometti et al. Sotiriou suggests asking a gallery whether the piece represents something essential about that practice. Ameti notes that value shouldn’t be defined by price alone. “We look at the quality of the work, the artist’s approach, and whether there’s something about the object that stays with you,” she said. “We always prefer someone to buy one piece they genuinely love rather than several pieces simply because they seem like a good deal.” Seed Deposit (II), 2026 Anna May Kirk COMA Edition status matters more at this scale than for most other media. An edition is a fixed number of near-identical copies cast from one original, with the total set in advance by the artist. Open editions have no limit to the number produced, which is why they often cost less. A bronze in an edition of three is a meaningfully different object from the same cast in an edition of 500. Ask how many were made, whether artist’s proofs or variations exist, whether the work is unique, and who fabricated it. Most handmade work is unique, however. “Clients should always ask if a sculpture is a multiple, but they will find that most handmade works of art are unique as it is impossible to replicate something handmade so precisely,” Feld said. Still, the first rule of art buying remains: purchase what you love. “For us, collecting should start with a genuine connection to the work. Everything else, including edition size, comes after that,” Ameti summed up.

title: The 2027 Met Gala theme is “extraORDINARY,” highlighting the beauty of the everyday.
summary: The Metropolitan Museum of Art has announced “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday” as the Costume Institute's spring 2027 exhibition. The exhibition will be on view May 9, 2027, through January 9, 2028, at the Met Fifth Avenue. The accompanying Met Gala fundraiser will take place Monday, May 3, 2027. This theme replaces the previous, now-canceled exhibition “ John Galliano : Horizons,” a planned retrospective that would have made Galliano the third living designer honored by the Costume Institute. The Met and Galliano jointly called off that show on August 31st, after weeks of criticism over Galliano's 2011 antisemitic and racist remarks, which had gotten him fined and fired from Dior. “extraORDINARY,” with its deliberately modest theme of jeans, T-shirts, and everyday materials, is a conspicuously low-key follow-up to a controversy that had centered on Galliano’s penchant for excesses. Drawing on the Costume Institute's collection alongside loans and new acquisitions, the show examines how designers rework familiar garments and ordinary materials— such as jeans, T-shirts, puffer coats, paper, plastic, metal—through craft, construction, and conceptual wit, while their earlier functions and histories remain embedded in what the new designs mean. “Fashion offers an immediate and compelling way to look at the world,” said Max Hollein, director and CEO of the museum. “By bringing together works that begin with the clothes, objects, and materials of daily life, extraORDINARY invites visitors to discover the creativity and ingenuity in things they encounter every day.” Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute's curator in charge, framed the show as a meditation on familiarity itself. “A pair of jeans, a white shirt, or a sweatshirt can hold traces of a life—the habits, memories, and attachments that make something our own. Designers work with that familiarity, revealing unexpected possibilities within forms and materials we think we already know," he said. Bolton has also described the show as a follow-up to this year's “Costume Art,” telling the New York Times that "each focuses on how clothes are worn." The exhibition, expected to bring together some 200 to 230 pieces including loans and pieces from the Costume Institute's archive, opens with garments from Jun Takahashi 's fall/winter 2024–25 Undercover collection “Watching a Working Woman,” inspired partly by Wim Wenders 's 2023 film Perfect Days . Two central sections follow. The first, “Familiar Forms,” groups archetypal garments—puffer coats, jeans, flannel shirts, and biker jackets—to trace how shifts in scale and material unsettle their recognizability. The second, “Common Matter,” is organized around paper, plastic, and metal, featuring works including a 1992 Rei Kawakubo dress for Comme des Garçons and a Helmut Lang jacket. The show closes with selections from Kunihiko Morinaga's Anrealage collections spanning 2009 to 2021, in which garments built around cubes, spheres, and pyramids probe how clothing accommodates—or fails to accommodate—the human body. The exhibition is made possible by Instagram, with major funding from Moncler and additional support from Condé Nast. The Met has not yet announced a dress code for the May 3rd benefit event, but Bolton has suggested it will follow the exhibition's understated register, a departure from the gala's more flamboyant past themes.

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Mmangaliso Nzuza
summary: Mmangaliso Nzuza wants his paintings to give off the feeling of home. One canvas in his Cape Town studio, As the Red-eyed Dove Sings (2025), takes its title from a bird whose song he remembers hearing as a child. “I wanted to almost capture that memory that it held for me,” he told us. “I want them to feel like what I feel when I think about home.” His paintings, which primarily depict human figures, are built from bold, angular forms that nod to Cubism . Nzuza became interested in how Picasso , Braque , and other Cubists drew on African masks and sculptural traditions. “This has almost been a way of reclaiming that into my culture,” he reflected. Held Voices, 2026 Mmangaliso Nzuza Southern Guild Assembly, 2026 Mmangaliso Nzuza Southern Guild During breaks from painting, he takes long walks, gathering impressions of his surroundings before returning to his studio in Woodstock, where Table Mountain rises in the distance. There, he prefers to dive straight into painting rather than plan his compositions. “Going straight onto the canvas allows my innermost emotions to flow,” he explained. Nzuza’s rise has been swift. He began painting in earnest during the pandemic in 2020, when his mother bought him paints and encouraged his artistic inclinations. He started sharing his work on Instagram, and it quickly drew attention. He later connected with Southern Guild , which presented his first solo exhibition in Cape Town in 2024. Hymn in Iridescence, 2025 Mmangaliso Nzuza Southern Guild In April 2026, his exhibition “Ballad of the Peacock” helped inaugurate the gallery’s new Tribeca space and marked his U.S. solo debut. His work has since appeared at Frieze London and The Armory Show and entered the collections of the North Dakota Museum of Art and the Montecito Contemporary Art Collection. He’ll also be featured at Art Basel Miami Beach in December. We caught up with Nzuza in his studio, where he shared his work, process, and inspirations. “I would describe my work as something that invokes a feeling, a memory,” he said. “Most importantly, I want it to feel familiar.” Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . title: teamLab to open first US museum in Southern California.
summary: teamLab , the Tokyo-based art collective known for immersive, technology-driven installations, will open its first permanent museum in the United States in Anaheim, California. The museum will be located in OCVIBE, a 100-acre entertainment and arts district currently under construction. The museum will span approximately 110,000 square feet, with architecture by the Los Angeles firm smith-clementi. It is expected to open in 2030. “It is with great joy that we announce the opening of teamLab's first major museum in North America, located at OCVIBE in Anaheim,” said Toshiyuki Inoko, teamLab’s founder. “People immerse themselves with their entire bodies, transcending the boundaries between themselves, the artworks, and the world around them, becoming part of a borderless continuity.” The move follows the opening of teamLab’s Abu Dhabi location last year and adds to a museum in Singapore and five branches in Japan. The California museum will anchor one end of OCVIBE, which is being designed to integrate art, dining, and entertainment throughout its public spaces rather than treating culture as a separate amenity. “Bringing teamLab to OCVIBE reflects the importance we've placed on integrating arts and culture into the district's master plan,” said Dan Young, OCVIBE's executive director of development. “It adds an entirely new dimension to what people can experience here in Anaheim, while helping establish OCVIBE as a cultural destination for California and the U.S." Because teamLab’s darkened, immersive galleries require a largely windowless structure, smith-clementi designed the museum's exterior as what the firm calls a shimmering cloak, with a textured, scale-like surface that shifts in color and appearance with the sunlight throughout the day. The building is conceived as a visual counterpoint to the neighboring, glass-walled Anaheim Regional Transportation Intermodal Center (ARTIC), which is solid and colorful by day, but designed to darken in the evening. “There's a feeling of transformation important to the exterior,” said Julie Smith-Clementi of smith-clementi. “This building feels different depending on the direction or pace of your approach... We want the design to leave room for imagination and discovery and, like in nature, to offer something new with each visit.” OCVIBE’s first phase is set to open in March 2027 with a 5,000-capacity concert hall, followed by the Katella Commons market hall and The Weave, the district’s office building, along with its first restaurants and public art program. The teamLab museum, slated for 2030, will follow as the district continues building out toward a planned 2033 completion.

title: 7 Contemporary Artists’ Tips for Surviving the Winter
summary: Shinjuku Gyoen in Winter, 2024 aryon Kyoto Art Gallery As winter approaches, the days grow shorter, leaves disappear from the trees, and falling temperatures invite us to retreat indoors. With the clocks turned back and darkness arriving earlier, the changing season feels especially pronounced. But while the natural world slows down, the art world moves in the opposite direction. The exhibition calendar remains busy as the year draws to a close, with galleries, museums, and auction houses bustling with activity. For artists, the colder months can bring intense productivity and mounting deadlines, even as the world outside their studios begins to quieten. Artist Mark Dion , who works in an upstate New York studio surrounded by forest, notes the contrasting rhythms. “In the rhythm of the natural world, everything is shutting down in the fall: Animals start to hibernate, and trees take all of their energy out of the leaves,” he said. “We are, however, back to work.” Yet for many artists, the changing seasons also bring fresh inspiration and opportunities to reconsider their relationship with the studio. “I start by collecting thoughts from my walks and wanderings, observing how the seasons change the landscape, how the way we dress shifts, and what nature is growing and offering,” explains New York–based artist Ian Ha . River side, 2024 Vahram Meliqsetyan Vayer Art Gallery For London-based painter Bex Massey , cooler temperatures are a welcome relief. “The disgusting levels of heat have abated, and I am keen to get paintings to a point of resolution for the new year,” she said. The changing atmosphere can also find its way into the work itself. For Rodolpho Parigi , who recently relocated from São Paulo to New York, the cooler, darker months echo the chromatic world of his paintings. “There’s something cooler, more ambiguous, slightly metallic about their atmosphere,” he said. Others see the season as a reminder to pause. London-based sculptor Magali Reus encourages making the most of the fleeting sunshine before winter sets in, while fellow artist Amba Sayal-Bennett offers a simpler piece of advice: “And the most important tip, I think: rest!” Artsy asked seven artists how they navigate the changing rhythms of the colder months, from the demands of the exhibition calendar to finding moments to slow down. Rodolpho Parigi B. 1977, São Paulo. Lives and works in São Paulo and New York. “Now that I’ve been living in New York for the last three months, the connection between my work and my studio has become much more apparent. Unlike São Paulo, New York has very distinct seasons. The shifts in temperature, light, and atmosphere are much more pronounced, and I find that these changes inevitably become part of my work. “The temperature of the studio, the quality of the light, and the landscape I encounter on my way to my studio inside the Elizabeth Foundation for the Arts all somehow find their way into the paintings. Black volumen Bestiaire # 32, 2024 Rodolpho Parigi Nara Roesler “At the moment, I’m developing a series of blue paintings, and I can already sense a relationship between their atmosphere and the environment in which they’re being made. I am working on a collaborative show between Nara Roesler and Anton Kern galleries for November, so having an exhibition ahead of me makes my priorities very clear.” Bex Massey B. 1985, Newcastle, U.K. Lives and works in London. “I spend the majority of my time in the studio, and my work has heaps of layers, so this works well with drying times. A chicken-and-egg situation, maybe? “The season means cooler temperatures, so reverting to a dreamy studio life. Now that my paintings at Seventeen Gallery’s Frieze London booth are out, I will be in the studio a bit less. William, 2022 Bex Massey Unit “To be more productive, I think you just need to ask yourself what kind of work and when works best for you…and try not to get thrown off by what other people are doing.” Magali Reus B. 1981, The Hague, Netherlands. Lives and works in London. “I try to find time for tidying and reorganizing my Shoreditch studio at the end of each working day. It is something I don’t enjoy doing, but I find it a helpful practice for working in a focused and careful way. It helps avoid damage and gives me more of an overview. That, and it feels great returning to a tidy space early the next day. “It is all dependent on what’s in the calendar. At the moment, it is quite a lot. Clementine (Sleepy Soils), 2024 Magali Reus Galerie Greta Meert Apricots, 2021 Magali Reus Mai 36 Galerie “There’s the exhibition ‘Swimming by Night’ at The Perimeter in London, with a new publication. There was a small book exhibition opening at Tenderbooks, Cecil Street, with all of my printed matter as well as some design objects I’ve been making. I designed a menu for Toklas, the delicious London restaurant; I showed work at Frieze London with The Approach and at Art Basel Paris with Mai 36 Galerie . And, lastly, I am opening a large-scale solo exhibition, ‘Tenant,’ at the Kunsthalle Wien in late November, where I will be showing over 80 works, all new or recent. “This exhibition will also feature a new publication, which we’re finessing at the moment. So, in short, a very busy time of year! No complaints, though; it has been, and is, all wonderfully enjoyable and very rewarding!” Amba Sayal-Bennett B. 1991, London. Lives and works in London. “My relationship with my studio in Deptford is less seasonal and more project-based. Between shows, I spend a long time researching, which means I can work from anywhere. It’s towards the end of this process that I’m in the studio more consistently. “I’ve been developing a body of work exploring material afterlives within Western allopathic medicine. I’ve been particularly interested in how waste is governed and recuperated within this context. For example, I’ve been tracing how redundant National Health Service patient X-rays have been sold to the Royal Mint to be stripped of silver, converted into bullion, and then processed into jewelry. Some of this work was presented at Frieze London with Carbon12, and also as part of my solo show, ‘Vark,’ at Indigo+Madder in London. Webber, 2018 Amba Sayal-Bennett LUNDGREN GALLERY Taj, 2018 Amba Sayal-Bennett LUNDGREN GALLERY “I really enjoy autumn and its change of pace; I tend to feel more focused once it starts to get colder. I teach at University of the Arts London, so autumn marks the new academic year and a busier season. I tend to be more productive the busier I am and find that moving between different work and projects can be really generative.” Ian Ha B. 1997, Yong-in, South Korea. Lives and works in New York. “There is a sense of anticipation, especially when there’s an exhibition, ‘MacGuffin: Five Korean Artists and Five Writers from Art Omi’ at Space ZeroOne in New York. “I’m currently in the process of moving, so my studio feels less like a single, defined space and more like a collection of scattered islands, each ‘island’ serving a different purpose in my practice. There’s a certain beauty in working across these different stations; moving between them allows me to make unexpected connections and discover how each environment contributes something of its own to the work. We didn't mean to go to sea, 2023 Ian Ha PLATO Gallery Lost, 2023 Ian Ha Fragment “I encountered and read Nadia Owusu’s Aftershocks , and it organically unlocked a new layer of meaning in the work I had made earlier this spring. I realized more fully how time and seasonal shifts have a way of reframing the work. Connecting with Nadia grew into a layered exchange, and that collaboration is coming to life with our MacGuffin exhibition. “My tip to readjust to the new season is to find the right music, and adopt a plant.” Sophie Treppendahl B. 1991, Louisiana. Lives and works in New Orleans. “My studio has frequently been a muse in my own paintings. Each year, I typically create one large painting of my studio space to capture the year’s work. The studio paintings include the work I have in progress at the time and the books of artists inspiring my current work, and serve as a time capsule of my state of mind during that period. Some paintings are bright and cheerful, others are quieter and more subdued. For me, these paintings function as a series of self-portraits over the years. “Right now I am finishing up paintings for a solo exhibition at SOCO Gallery in Charlotte [North Carolina] opening in November, and a few pieces for Art Basel Miami with Philip Martin Gallery. Each New Year after my busy season, I clean the studio thoroughly and repaint the studio floor. It’s a nice way to purge the previous year and have a momentarily clean space. Living Room, Evening, 2021 Sophie Treppendahl Romer Young Gallery “My year-round studio hack is audiobooks. I listen to cheesy thriller audiobooks while I work. There is something about the ‘whodunit’ book that keeps me focused while I paint. I strive for work-life balance even during the busiest times. When I leave the studio, I try to leave my entire work brain behind. I go on long walks with my toddler at the park after my workday and count down to the joy ahead—finishing deadlines and seeing family for the holidays.” Mark Dion B. 1961, Massachusetts. Lives and works in Copake, New York. “I’m a really big birdwatcher, so I try to take advantage of the migration season, which is always a little melancholic, as fall is, because instead of saying hello to birds like you do in the spring, now is the time to say goodbye to them until the springtime. There is undoubtedly a kind of melancholic aspect to this season. “This is the time when I’m gathering pine cones, acorns, chestnuts, and all of these things which are now mature and dropping from the trees. They come in handy later on at the studio. Some Recent Plagues (framed), 2025 Mark Dion Obee Editions “I live in an upstate town called Copake, surrounded by forest. My studio actually was one of my sculptures, one of my follies from the exhibition I did at Storm King , ‘The Field Station of the Melancholy Marine Biologist.’ This was a freestanding wooden house that you could not enter, but could look through the large windows and see everything inside, which was filled to look like a marine biologist’s laboratory. Fall is, however, a tricky time because the structure is not insulated or heated, so we are in the final weeks that I can use my studio. Then my dining room table becomes my studio until spring. “My new solo exhibition, ‘Eccentric Collectors Like Us,’ at Concord Museum in Massachusetts, displays objects from almost a thousand repurposed boxes that filled my studio. Each of them contains toys, old wooden tools, game pieces, and ceramic bits. I lined them with felt or antique paper and found the right object to put inside.”

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Donyel Ivy-Royal
summary: From street corners and vintage cars to his family’s home, Donyel Ivy-Royal paints the world that’s close to him. The Brooklyn-based artist transforms everyday subjects into large, layered paintings, giving each what he calls “their own monument.” His process begins with his own snapshots of his neighborhood and his family, and he isn't particularly concerned with getting the perfect shot. “I like the ones that come out blurry, overexposed, or underexposed. It works for what I’m doing,” he told us. In the studio, he builds up and scrapes away layers of paint until familiar scenes take shape, resembling the hazy quality of memory. Highway 101, Southbound, 2026 Donyel Ivy-Royal Jack Shainman Gallery Born in Portland, Oregon, Ivy-Royal came up in the city’s DIY music and art scene, and his practice spans painting, photography, music, poetry, and installation. A four-track recorder is not far from his canvas and paints, and music is often part of his studio routine. The rhythms of the music carry into the gestures of painting. Ivy-Royal’s career has gained momentum recently. In January 2026, he joined Jack Shainman Gallery ’s roster after working there as an art handler. Soon after, he had his first New York solo exhibition at David Peter Francis, and in May, he presented a buzzy solo booth with Jack Shainman at Independent. On November 5th, he opens his debut solo with Jack Shainman Gallery, “ By the time the rain comes, we will be home ,” in Chelsea. The exhibition features new paintings and an installation that turns a wall in the gallery into the front of a building, a nod to the surfaces he drew on as a child. Tedi’s gourds that look like birds, 2026 Donyel Ivy-Royal Jack Shainman Gallery There is a warm rain, that becomes a flower, 2026 Donyel Ivy-Royal Jack Shainman Gallery We caught up with Ivy-Royal at his Brooklyn studio, joining him for a morning walk with his dog before heading into the studio. “My process is so much an appreciation of my own life,” he told us. “I hope that people leave and appreciate their own thing, and feel inspired to take pictures, or go tag their neighborhood, or paint a picture, or leave the hood, or don’t leave the hood and make art.” Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . title: Julie Curtiss Paints a Twisted Love Letter to New York City
summary: Julie Curtiss is finally painting her metropolitan fever dream. “It’s a New York painting story,” said Curtiss, during a recent conversation at her East Williamsburg studio. On the studio walls were her most recent paintings: scenes of faceless women doing yoga in small apartments, the neon lights of storefronts, a laundromat. “I decided the show would be a little vignette of life in New York, and of what it is to feel like you’re getting older in the city,” she said. The artist has earned acclaim over the past decade for her distinctive style synthesizing Pop and Surrealist sensibilities with the bold patterning and controlled sensuality of Chicago Imagists like Christina Ramberg . She is a painter of glistening coils of long hair, of rippled shellfish, and of fur-covered food in the lineage of Meret Oppenheim . Born and raised in Paris, she is the only child of a French librarian mother and a Vietnamese technical photographer father. But New York has been her home for the past 16 years, and the backdrop of a career from early jobs as a studio assistant for KAWS and Jeff Koons to her 2017 breakout at Spring/Break Art Show, followed by exhibitions at prominent galleries including Anton Kern Gallery and White Cube . She married and became a mother in the city. Today she lives just a short walk from her studio. Now, for the first time in five years, she’s opening a New York solo show—and in grand form. “Unreal,” which opens November 10th, will mark Curtiss’s first New York solo show with Gagosian . It is her first New York solo exhibition since “Somnambules” at Anton Kern Gallery in the fall of 2022. But the exhibition is not an uncomplicated love letter to New York. Instead, Curtiss leans into the chaos, control, and excess that define a city acclaimed architect Le Corbusier once described as a “fairy catastrophe.” “We get here in our twenties and thirties, full of energy and ambition,” she said. “Then, as time goes on, the city wears you out. You make all those attempts at renewal, and it becomes about maintenance, about just trying to keep up with that crazy pace.” Curtiss’s last solo exhibition, “Maid in Feathers,” which opened at White Cube in Seoul in November 2025, dealt with the transformation and complex realities of early motherhood rendered in gothic-feeling black-and-white paintings of breast pumps, bassinets, and bath times. Here, she found herself grappling with a more vague sense of identity. “That show [“Maid in Feathers”] practically painted itself. It was very cohesive: the same palette throughout, all about motherhood, very dreamy and surrealist,” she said. “This show was different. It was the New York show, where everybody was going to be and see it. I felt I had to do something great and I went in a lot of different directions.” Ultimately, Curtiss arrived at a language that she describes as “magical realist” as opposed to the Surrealist visions that appeared in earlier works. While the comically macabre images of monstrous, manicured claws and heads on platters of her earlier works are absent, a winking sense of strangeness still abounds. “It’s everyday life, and where it meets unreality,” she said. “It’s also about thinking about our relationship to images right now—you can’t trust images representing the world. These paintings are very mundane scenes, but they all have something a little off about them, something slightly funny or an unexpected juxtaposition.” In the painting Grand Street (2026), neon lights illuminate a Chinatown storefront in which a Peking duck hangs in the windows next to tanks of clams, crab, and fish. But these animals are not oblivious to their circumstances. Instead they stare out at the viewers with hyperaware urgency. “Everything [in the show] is imbued with so much projection,” she said. “The animals carry so much human projection. They become stand-ins for human emotion, or for humanity.” The paintings often take inspiration from scenes in Curtiss’s everyday life—her local bodega, a window strung with Christmas lights on her block, and a nearby psychic’s parlor. “My life is very local,” said Curtiss. “My life is studio, home, park, studio, home, park.” But in these familiar stomping grounds, a sense of urgency and intensity exist. “It’s this ‘only in New York’ energy, with crazy stuff happening all the time. There’s the constant contrast of the high and the low, socially and economically,” said Curtiss. “With all that friction, there’s always something coming out of it. It’s also exhausting, but it’s alive.” Her female figures, faces always obscured, become a stand-in for this tension between urban luxury and decay. A hole appears in the stocking of an elegantly clad woman, for instance. In the painting Makeover (2026), two women in fur coats and oversized sunglasses, their hair perfectly coiffed and nails manicured, face away from the viewer. One smokes a cigarette. Their faces are swathed in the white bandages that immediately signal recent plastic surgery. They are elegant and mangled at once. “For a while, in my social media feed, I was getting mostly skin-care tricks to take care of your skin and limit the damage of life. The façade. It’s funny, because a few of these paintings are about that never-ending, high-maintenance work,” said Curtiss. Curtiss’s women—practicing yoga, getting nipped and tucked, and playing the perfect housewife—try to wrest control from the unpredictability of aging and life in a city with its own out-of-date infrastructure. But Curtiss is also finding new freedom within this push and pull of chaos and control. Her process for these works has been much more intuitive than in the past, with the artist sometimes discovering her subject matter as she works through it in some cases. Her works have become more nuanced, too. Whereas Curtiss often used to leave her backgrounds empty, here she plunges viewers into complex spaces. Her airtight control of pattern has given way to movement—plumes of smoke, sheens and reflections of washing machines and windows. “Maybe it’s just natural development, but things become a little more complex—themes are a little deeper, and my frame is getting a little wider, too,” she said. “I used to be really focused on a single object, and it was a bit like boom, boom, boom. Now I’m playing more with composition. Everything is more sophisticated.” Those shifts are, perhaps, the result of living and working in a city that is constantly asking its people to grow and adapt. Curtiss, for one, is energized by the thought of sharing this work in the city and, in typical New York fashion, getting some honest opinions back. “New York people are very driven; you can’t live in New York if you’re not really driven,” she said. “These people engage with the work and give you thorough feedback. New York people are pretty serious when it comes to art.”

title: Stella McCartney and Yoshitomo Nara unveil limited-edition collection.
summary: Designer Stella McCartney and artist Yoshitomo Nara have teamed up for a third limited-edition collaboration. The collection, themed around a "rock'n'roll forest," spans ready-to-wear, handbags, shoes, and accessories, featuring Nara's childlike figures and animal motifs across artisan knitwear in responsibly sourced wool, organic cotton jersey separates, handcrafted vegan bags, and graphic-printed trainers. The partnership extends McCartney and Nara’s ongoing creative partnership, which the brand describes as rooted in a shared commitment to nature, animals, and individuality. The collection is made with what McCartney describes as “100 percent responsible” materials. The collaboration also includes four exclusive, made-to-order styles produced in very limited quantities by the brand’s atelier, including vegan handbags, framed hand-crocheted portraits based on archival Nara artworks, and hand-knitted scarves and jumpers. The framed portraits are individually crocheted and then embroidered to build texture and dimension. The jumpers, embroidered with Nara's Cutie in the Puddle (2024) , combine multiple yarns, stitches, and both hand and machine techniques, with each piece taking more than 60 hours to complete. Meanwhile, each scarf requires roughly 40 hours of artisanal work. The collection also includes anStella McCartney x Yoshitomo Nara adidas SPW64 sneaker. The sneaker reworks the Tokyo 64 track shoe in lightweight recycled materials printed with Nara's artwork, with a tongue inspired by a 1956 Melbourne Olympics shoe design. In Shinjuku, Tokyo, a four-week pop-up will open November 11th at the gallery Isetan The Space with an installation and activations on view through December 8th. The Isetan pop-up will release a different exclusive Nara sticker each week, while select Stella McCartney boutiques internationally will offer their own city-specific sticker designs. The limited-edition collection launches globally on November 11th on the Stella McCartney website and at boutiques and retailers worldwide, following an exclusive presale. Select exclusive styles will also be available in Japan and at the brand's SoHo boutique in New York, with further location-specific availability to be announced.

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Aiza Ahmed
summary: There’s an infectious energy to Aiza Ahmed ’s work, from her fluid, expressive figures to the humor and theatricality she brings to explorations of masculinity and belonging. It all begins with blind-contour drawing: putting pen to paper without looking down, trusting her eyes to observe and her hands to sketch away. Over the past year, Ahmed took part in the Fire Station artist residency in Doha, Qatar, where she was immediately drawn to the waterfront and the men she encountered around the city, from boatmen to Uber drivers. “I was noticing a very different kind of masculinity that was more tender, that was soft, something that I hadn’t experienced before,” she told Artsy. She began capturing their likenesses. Those drawings become the foundation for paintings, textile installations, and carved wood sculptures. Across her practice, Ahmed explores the Indian subcontinent, its borders, migration, and histories, drawing on real narratives while imagining her own. The art world is taking notice. Ahmed’s work has recently been acquired by ICA Miami , Qatar Museums, and the Pérez Art Museum Miami . In February 2026, she presented a new body of work at the inaugural Art Basel Qatar , where she was the youngest artist with a solo presentation. She also recently participated in New York’s closely watched Silver Art residency program. How to build a man, 2026 Aiza Ahmed Nature Morte This week, she’s featured in Fire Station’s inaugural Artists Intensive Study Programme exhibition, curated by Egyptian artist Wael Shawky , and soon she’ll have a show in Paris with MASSIMODECARLO . We caught up with Ahmed at her studio in Doha before joining her for a day of drawing, which took her through the city in an Uber to the waterside, where she discussed some of the men who have inspired her work. title: 5 Standout Shows to See at Small Galleries This November
summary: Y el agua cae otra vez/And the Water Falls Again〈水再次落下〉, 2026 Ana Teresa Barboza NUNU FINE ART In this monthly roundup, we spotlight five stellar exhibitions at small and rising galleries. “ Afterglow: From the Residue of a Departed Sun ” Tabari , at No. 9 Frieze Cork Street, London Through Nov. 21 Barzakh #11, 2025 -2026 Mohamed Monaiseer Tabari Will the Gods Belong?, 8, 2023 Maitha Abdalla Tabari “ Afterglow ” brings together the work of four artists— Maitha Abdalla , Omar Kholeif , Mohamed Monaiseer , and Randa Maddah —as they explore the porous border between life and death through painting, spoken word and poetry, installation, mixed media, and sculpture. These works draw on diverse cosmologies, from Emirati folk narratives and the African trickster myth to Islamic metaphysics. Egyptian artist Monaiseer presents delicate, constellation-like paintings of botanical forms on cotton fabric, while Emirati artist Abdalla paints gestural mythic scenes that blend animal and human forms. Kholeif, who is best known as a curator and author, paints reverie-like abstractions that hover at the edge of legibility, hinting at landscapes or figuration. Kholeif was born in Cairo to Egyptian and Sudanese parents, and raised between Glasgow and Los Angeles, among other places. His works are shaped by these diasporic experiences. Syrian Maddah, who was born in the occupied Golan Heights in 1983, paints mythic, mysterious paintings of women beings who merge into birds and trees. Maddah, who also creates puppets, films, and other media, imagines figures shaped by weighty psychological burdens. Presented at Dubai gallery Tabar i’s London space, the exhibition brings together an evocative range of creative voices from across the Middle East looking at mysteries of life, death, and the hereafter. Tony Huynh “ Heaven or Las Vegas ” Galerie Christian Lethert , Cologne Nov. 6–Dec. 18 As Days Go By, 2026 Tony Huynh Galerie Christian Lethert American painter Tony Huynh makes his European solo debut with “ Heaven or Las Vegas ,” his first show with Galerie Christian Lethert . His small-format oil paintings on wood draw from centuries of art history, particularly outsider art , as well as techniques from Japanese printmaking. Working in a restrained palette, Huynh portrays playful, almost childlike visions—a woman in a blue dress reading, a cow in a bucolic landscape, or a small child with a toboggan—that carry an air of solitude and loneliness. In one painting, As Days Go By (2026), a woman is shown from above resting fully clothed on a bed. Her face is blank and featureless, and her bed appears almost book-like in its form. The painting echoes the pithy and poetic works of Milton Avery. Huynh was born in 1986 in San Francisco and lives and works in Sacramento. He earned his BFA at the California College of the Arts. His previous solo exhibitions include “Magical Thinking” (2025) at PABLO´S BIRTHDAY in New York, “A Summer’s Dream” (2024) at Scroll NYC Gallery in New York, and “Bay Vistas” (2023) at Bryant Street Gallery in Palo Alto, California. Ana Teresa Barboza “ A Message From Water ” NUNU Fine Art , New York Nov. 6–Jan. 9 Camino a la montaña/Path to the Mountain〈通往山的路〉, 2026 Ana Teresa Barboza NUNU FINE ART Entre las hojas/Between the Leaves〈在葉子之間), 2026 Ana Teresa Barboza NUNU FINE ART Peruvian artist Ana Teresa Barboza draws from the landscape of her homeland in her fourth exhibition with NUNU FINE ART —her second in New York. Her mixed-media textile works render botanical forms from alpaca wool, Peruvian cotton, agave fiber, bronze, and photography. Barboza has structured this exhibition as a visual diary, tracing an eastward journey across Peru, from the forests of the Utcubamba Valley to Gocta Waterfall in the Amazonas region. She has extensively studied traditional methods of producing plant-based fibers and natural dyes from local communities. Her dyes come from native plants that she pulverizes and boils, tying the works back to the ecosystem they came from. The centerpiece of the exhibition is Y el agua cae otra vez/And the Water Falls Again (2026), a massive, vividly colored textile work with a cascading form that evokes a waterfall moving through the cloud forest. Barboza was born in 1981 in Lima. She studied at the Faculty of Art of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru and has completed residencies in Melbourne, Geneva, Paris, and Taipei. She won first prize in the Central Reserve Bank of Peru’s Second National Painting Competition in 2010 and the MAC National Art and Innovation Award in 2019. Peter Mohall “ När blommorna blommar ” QB Gallery , Oslo Through Nov. 29 Blomsterstilleben på en odde, 2026 Peter Mohall QB Gallery Untitled (brushstrokes painting), 2026 Peter Mohall QB Gallery Norwegian Swedish artist Peter Mohall juxtaposes landscapes and still life in uncanny compositions. Here, vases of flowers sit directly on rocks in the terrain or in front of windows that offer a panoramic view of nature. These landscape paintings, made with acrylic composite and painted in egg-oil tempera are purposely artificial, with their exaggerated and oversaturated hues. On the edge of several paintings is a control strip–like bands of color to each of the works, as if they were printed, underscoring their constructed nature. In two untitled works, the artist paints these test strip–like squiggles of color on otherwise bare linen canvases, heightening this photographic effect, reading like two blank negatives. Mohall was born in 1979 in Löddeköpinge, Sweden, and lives and works in Nesoddtangen, outside Oslo. He graduated from the Oslo National Academy of Fine Arts and received a 2015 grant from the Ellen Trotzig Foundation at the Malmö Art Museum. He has had solo exhibitions with Luce Gallery in Turin, Koki Arts in Tokyo, Pablo’s Birthday in New York, and QB Gallery , and his work is in the collections of Fondazione 107 in Turin, the Central Bank of Norway, and the JP Morgan Chase Collection. Quim Bové “ Levitation ” Bonner David Galleries , Scottsdale, Arizona Nov. 5–Dec. 19 "The Horizon is Not Too Far II", 2026 Quim Bové Bonner David Galleries "Levitation XII", 2026 Quim Bové Bonner David Galleries Quim Bové creates bold compositions in pigment, acrylic, and resin, often pairing target-like patterns with gestural splashes of color. Bové has said that he hopes these paintings invite an emotional response rather than a fixed interpretation. “When you feel, you don’t think,” he said in a gallery statement. Bové has been working for more than three decades and his works pull from philosophy, metaphysics, science, music, and drawing. His interests in classical music, jazz, and improvisation are foundational to his intuitive approach in which gesture becomes a way of thinking. Now living in the American Southwest, Bové also takes inspiration from the terrain’s vastness, intense light, and silence. Born in Catalonia, Bové taught himself to paint. He has had more than 30 solo exhibitions, and his work has been shown across the United States and Europe, including his recent series “Architecture of the Universe.” In 1995, he founded the conceptual art group Andorran Currency.
